title: System One: fast, structured decisions for software (documentation)
why: The vendor's definition of a decision model: state in, typed answers with calibrated probabilities out, no text. Read first. Secondary source.

title: AI primer: why decision models are trained for calibrated probabilities (documentation)
why: The vendor's contrast of RLHF, RLVR and its own RLCD, and its definition of calibration. The only public description of the training objective. Secondary source.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
why: The System 1 / System 2 metaphor the category borrows its name from. Book; secondary source for the deck's purposes.

title: Thinking fast and slow in AI
why: The AAAI framing of fast, automatic components beside slow, deliberate ones in AI systems; the intellectual ancestor of 'System One models'.

title: Distilling System 2 into System 1
why: Compressing deliberate reasoning into direct answers; where it works and where (GSM8K chain of thought) it fails. The closest academic cousin of a decision model's promise.

title: Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
why: Which classical learners are calibrated out of the box and which need Platt or isotonic correction. Calibrated classification predates deep learning. ICML 2005.

title: Measuring massive multitask language understanding
why: MMLU and the convention of scoring options by the log-probability of the answer letter: the first widely used 'decision readout' from a generative model.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
why: InstructGPT: the reward model (a decision model in all but name) and the RLHF pipeline that later work shows erodes calibration. TypeSafe's CEO is a co-author.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
why: LLM judges agree with humans over 80% of the time and show position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases; the generative route to decisions and its known faults.

title: Why language models hallucinate
why: Hallucination as classification error plus an evaluation culture that rewards guessing over abstention; the argument a calibrated, abstaining decision model answers.

title: Primitives: Choice, Score, Noul, Box (documentation)
why: The four question types, their answer shapes, and how to choose among them. Secondary source.

title: Confidence (documentation)
why: The exact confidence formulas for Choice and Score, the worked examples on slides 6-7, the three-band threshold advice. Secondary source.

title: State (documentation)
why: How to structure the content a question is asked about; facts in the state, judgments in the questions. Secondary source.

title: How to build with System One (documentation)
why: Code in control, narrow atomic questions, what/not_for/examples per option, batching, routing on confidence. Secondary source.

title: System One API reference and request rules (documentation)
why: Request and response shapes, limits (64k per request, 32k per question, 32 MiB body), headers for images and long context, status codes. Secondary source.

title: Cookbook: parallel questions (documentation)
why: Thirteen questions over a 53,777-character article in one call versus thirteen calls: 12.2x cheaper, 10x faster, answers identical on 11 of 13 and equally noisy on the rest. The batching evidence on slide 9. Secondary source.

title: Decisions API: Jev and the decision-model category (documentation)
why: The cross-vendor decisions endpoint, the catalog of decision models, and the warning that thresholds do not transfer across models. Secondary source.

title: Decisions API guide (documentation)
why: OpenAI's version of the same primitives (predicate, choice, score, refusal) on gpt-6-luna; no calibration claim, thresholds to be set from your own labels. Secondary source.

title: Batch prompting: efficient inference with large language model APIs
why: Many questions in one generative call: up to 5x token and time savings, with accuracy degrading as the batch grows. The academic precedent for fan-out, and the contrast with a decision model's independent questions.

title: Multi-task inference: can large language models follow multiple instructions at once?
why: Evaluating several instructions in a single pass; speedups and the conditions under which quality holds.

title: G-Eval: NLG evaluation using GPT-4 with better human alignment
why: Scoring with the probability-weighted sum over rating tokens instead of the argmax: the same construction as the Score primitive's expected level.

title: Leveraging large language models for multiple choice question answering
why: Multiple-choice symbol binding: present the options jointly and read the symbol. The readout that a Choice question formalizes.

title: On calibration of modern neural networks
why: Modern deep networks are overconfident where 1990s networks were not; reliability diagrams, ECE, and temperature scaling. The paper every LLM calibration study cites. ICML 2017.

title: Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation
why: The theory of scoring rules under which reporting the true belief is the unique optimum: why Brier and log loss can serve as training rewards. JASA 2007.

title: The comparison and evaluation of forecasters
why: The calibration-refinement decomposition and the reliability diagram. The Statistician 1983.

title: Probabilistic outputs for support vector machines and comparisons to regularized likelihood methods
why: Platt scaling: a sigmoid fitted to classifier scores; temperature scaling is its one-parameter special case.

title: Measuring calibration in deep learning
why: The choice of calibration metric re-ranks methods; adaptive binning, class conditioning and L2 variants of ECE. The pitfalls row on slide 26.

title: Verified uncertainty calibration
why: Scaling methods look better calibrated than they are; scaling-then-binning gives a verifiable estimate with known sample complexity.

title: Beyond temperature scaling: obtaining well-calibrated multiclass probabilities with Dirichlet calibration
why: Multiclass calibration as a linear map on log-probabilities, and class-wise ECE; relevant to Choice questions with many options.

title: Revisiting the calibration of modern neural networks
why: Architecture is a major determinant of calibration; some recent architectures are among the best calibrated. Calibration is not a monotone function of size.

title: A unifying theory of distance from calibration
why: ECE is discontinuous; consistent, smooth distance-from-calibration measures. STOC 2023.

title: Can you trust your model's uncertainty? Evaluating predictive uncertainty under dataset shift
why: Post-hoc calibration degrades under distribution shift; the warning behind 'calibrate on your own data'.

authors: Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein and Singh
title: Calibrate before use: improving few-shot performance of language models
why: A content-free input exposes a label prior in LLM classifiers; correcting it adds up to 30 points of accuracy and cuts prompt variance.

title: Language models (mostly) know what they know
why: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format, can predict P(True) of their own samples, and lose calibration when the format shifts.

title: GPT-4 technical report
why: Figure 8: the pre-trained model is well calibrated on an MMLU subset and the PPO-tuned model is not; the sentence 'post-training hurts calibration significantly'.

title: Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
why: GPT-3 fine-tuned to state a verbal probability is calibrated and remains moderately calibrated under distribution shift; CalibratedMath.

title: Just ask for calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence scores from language models fine-tuned with human feedback
why: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence beats the conditional token probability, cutting ECE by up to two-thirds (gpt-3.5, TriviaQA: 0.140 to 0.050).

title: Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs
why: A black-box elicitation framework (prompting, sampling, aggregation); LLMs remain overconfident and cluster their stated numbers.

title: On the calibration of large language models and alignment
why: Pretraining improves calibration with scale; instruction tuning worsens it, more so with synthetic data.

title: Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
why: Prompting is not enough; about a thousand graded examples and LoRA on internal features give uncertainty estimates that generalize.

title: Restoring calibration for aligned large language models: a calibration-aware fine-tuning approach
why: Preference collapse as the mechanism by which alignment destroys calibration, and a fine-tuning objective that restores it.

title: Calibration as a first-class criterion in LLM evaluation
why: A position paper: none of nine recent model reports report calibration at all.

title: 'My answer is C': first-token probabilities do not match text answers in instruction-tuned language models
why: For instruction-tuned models the first-token probability disagrees with the generated text answer at rates reaching over 60%: the central caveat for logprob readouts.

authors: Yang, Klein, Celikyilmaz, Peng and Tian
title: RLCD: reinforcement learning from contrastive distillation for language model alignment
why: The other RLCD: preference pairs from positive and negative prompts, for alignment. Nothing to do with calibration; included so the name collision is not mistaken for a source. ICLR 2024.

title: Reducing conversational agents' overconfidence through linguistic calibration
why: The earliest linguistic-calibration training signal for dialogue agents.

title: Linguistic calibration of long-form generations
why: Calibration defined through the decisions a reader makes from the text; supervised then RL training on a decision-based reward.

title: LACIE: listener-aware finetuning for confidence calibration in large language models
why: Calibration as preference optimization against a simulated listener; fewer wrong answers accepted by humans.

title: SaySelf: teaching LLMs to express confidence with self-reflective rationales
why: Supervised fine-tuning on self-reflective rationales followed by PPO with a quadratic confidence reward.

title: Taming overconfidence in LLMs: reward calibration in RLHF
why: Reward models prefer high stated confidence; two fixes inside the standard RLHF pipeline. Why preference rewards are not proper scoring rules.

title: Rewarding doubt: a reinforcement learning approach to calibrated confidence expression of large language models
why: RL with a log-scoring-rule reward on stated confidence; the optimal policy is exactly calibrated. The cleanest statement of the principle behind a calibration objective.

title: Beyond binary rewards: training LMs to reason about their uncertainty
why: RLCR: correctness plus a Brier score on the verbalized confidence; ordinary RL hurts calibration, RLCR improves it at no accuracy cost. The nearest published analogue of the vendor's 'RL for calibrated decisions'.

title: Reasoning models better express their confidence
why: Reasoning models are better calibrated in most settings tested, attributed to slow-thinking behaviours.

title: Reasoning about uncertainty: do reasoning models know when they don't know?
why: The counterpoint: reasoning models are overconfident on wrong answers, and deeper reasoning can make it worse.

title: Thinking out loud: do reasoning models know when they're right?
why: A 'reasoning tax': RL and distillation improve calibration on reasoning tasks but erode awareness of knowledge boundaries.

title: AbstentionBench: reasoning LLMs fail on unanswerable questions
why: Twenty datasets and twenty models; fine-tuning for reasoning degrades abstention by about a quarter on average.

title: Distilling the knowledge in a neural network
why: Soft targets as the training signal; the original recipe for compressing a large model's probabilities into a small one.

title: Distilling step-by-step! Outperforming larger language models with less training data and smaller model sizes
why: A 770M model trained on a large model's rationales beats 540B few-shot with a fraction of the data; distillation into a decision-sized model.

title: Knowledge distillation in automated annotation: supervised text classification with LLM-generated training labels
why: Classifiers trained on GPT-4 labels match those trained on human labels across 14 tasks; the cheapest route to a private decision model.
